topic.title: Stories are posted for one viewer
topic.claim: Half the stories we post aren't for our followers; they're for one person, and the viewer list is how we check.
topic.moment: You post a sunset story and open it four times in an hour to see if they've seen it.

turn.believed: We post stories to share our day.
turn.actually: We post them to send a message without sending a message.

topic.feeling: Caught, because this is exactly what I did last night.
topic.villain: A feature that shows you exactly who watched.
topic.because: The viewer list turns posting into a way to check on someone. It's safer than texting, because you never have to admit you cared.
topic.payoff: Look at your last five stories and ask who each one was really for.
topic.behaviour: People post stories and repeatedly check the viewer list for specific names.
topic.mechanism: Seeing who viewed gives a safe signal without direct contact.
topic.send_to: The friend who posted a very specific song story after a breakup.
topic.why_now: Stories are now how most people stay in touch, more than posts or texts.

score.why: Stories posted for one person, and the viewer list is the check. Caught-in-the-act humour with a real turn.

violations: Slide 7: "Anyone who has built an app knows a screen people refresh all evening is a screen worth keeping." This is a hidden-motive claim stated as fact (Instagram keeps the viewer list on purpose to drive engagement). It is not in the sources, and it also leans on the writer's builder background in a pure-observation post (lived is false). Fails the mechanism-can't-be-shown rule and the credentials rule.

Slide 6: the slide is a bare fact ("Instagram says the viewer list isn't simply in order of who watched first") with no payoff of its own. Slide 7 then uses it to undercut the reader's theory, but the pair reads as a data explainer inserted mid-post. The sourced fact itself is fine, but slide 6 is close to a dead slide as written.

Slide 3 and slide 5 overlap: slide 3 says stories are a text we were too proud to send, and slide 5 explains again that a story is safer than a text because it needs no reply. Slide 5 restates the idea in new words. Slide 3 also states the turn before the examples show it, so slide 4 reads as a list of proof for something already conceded.

Slide 8: "It's not desperation. It's the safest way to say 'I miss you' or 'look, I'm doing great'." It restates slide 5's 'safer than a text' point a third time. It is a dead slide apart from the closer "Deniability, with a filter on it."

Feeling/villain: the topic's villain is the feature that shows who watched, but the post barely blames it. Slide 7 hints at it with an unsupported motive claim. Slide 6's sourced fact never lands as a sting, so the reader is caught on slide 2 and then lectured on mechanism instead of made to feel more.
notes: Slide 7: delete "Anyone who has built an app knows a screen people refresh all evening is a screen worth keeping." It claims a deliberate motive Instagram has not stated and borrows the author's builder background. Replace it with what the source supports. The viewer list can't reliably show whether that one person watched, so the signal you're chasing is noisy. The sting is that you've been reading tea leaves.

Slides 3, 5, 8: the 'safer than a text' idea is said three times. Keep it once, in slide 5, where it has the best wording ("officially, you just posted a sunset"). Make slide 3 only set the turn (stories are for one person), and cut the first half of slide 8 so it carries only "Deniability, with a filter on it." Merge or remove one slide to tighten the post.

Slide 6: it is a fact with no stake. Merge it with slide 7 into one slide: the viewer list isn't strictly ordered by who watched first, so the name at the top proves nothing, yet you built a theory on it anyway. Put the human reaction ("you've read meaning into the order of faces") after the fact so it lands as a laugh, not a footnote.

Slide 4: the three examples are good, but the third ("a 'random' story from the café you two used to go to") is the only one that shows the checking behaviour. Add one insider detail with a sense beyond sight (the phone buzzing on the table, the thumb hovering over the eye icon) so it reads like someone who has done this, and sharpen the examples so they cover people who aren't only post-breakup.

Slide 2: the opening scene is strong, but "a page that sells kurtas" is a throwaway. Replace it with the viewer-list detail only a person who has done this would notice, like scrolling past the same three names and checking whether the grey 'seen' tick is there. violations: Slide 1 (hook): 'We post stories to send a message without sending one.' is the topic's turn stated flat, but the cover headline retains a leftover bracket '[send a message]' and the sub 'The sunset was never the point.' gives away the close; the cover is not clean (fails the cover clarity rule).

Slide 6: 'Instagram says the viewer list isn't simply in the order people watched...' is a sourced fact, but it is stated in a news-recap way and undercuts the turn: the post says the viewer list is how we check, then says the list proves little, with no because for why we keep checking anyway. The fact sits as a detour rather than backing the opinion (facts as hero risk, dead-ish slide).

Slide 2: 'Then you open your own story four times in an hour.' is fine as texture, but slide 2 and slide 3 stop short of showing the pattern: only the sunset, the Arijit song, the boarding pass and the thumb-hover are given, and the thumb-hover is a behaviour, not a story type, so there are really three examples, and the boarding pass ('the friend who said you'd never leave home') reads as a specific invented scenario about another person rather than a typical one (relatability thin, example too narrow).

Slide 4 (dead/over-explained): 'Because a text asks for a reply, and no reply is its own answer. A call feels like too much now, and a long text reads like a confession.' and slide 5 'A story asks for nothing. If their name shows up, you got your answer without ever admitting there was a question.' say the same idea twice (safer than texting); slide 5 should merge into slide 4.

This is a general, non-India source. I found no India-specific research backing or refuting the claim that half of stories are for one person.

cover.headline: We post stories to [send a message] without sending one
cover.sub: The sunset was never the point.

paragraphs: We post stories to send a message without sending one.
You'll say it's just a sunset.
Then you open your own story four times in an hour. Each time the screen lights up, your thumb goes to the viewer count first.
The list keeps growing, and you keep scrolling it for one name.
slides.why_swipe: What else counts as one of these stories?

paragraphs:
The sunset has cousins:
– the very specific Arijit song, lyrics on screen, a week after the breakup
– the gym mirror selfie or the "new job" post, meant for the ex or old boss
– the party story, posted for one friend who didn't invite you
The real ones go up at the hour that person is usually online. And if the wrong person views first, some get deleted.
Because a text can be ignored, and an ignored text stings. A story is deniable. If nothing comes back, you never asked anything.
It's a read receipt you never had to ask for.
slides.why_swipe: And if their name never shows up?

paragraphs: When the name isn't there by evening, nobody admits defeat. You post a second story. Better light, cooler song. Then you check again.
Two stories in, you still haven't sent them one word. That's the whole appeal.
slides.why_swipe: Does the order of names mean anything?

paragraphs: In 2018, Instagram said the viewer list is sorted by several signals, including who viewed recently. It isn't a ranking of who cares.
So where their name sits tells you nothing about them. You've been reading feelings into an order the app made.
slides.why_swipe: How do you know which of yours were for one person?

paragraphs: Go through your last five stories and name who each one was really for.
The viewer count was never your audience. One name in it was.

end.save: Come back to this the next time you open your own story for the third time.
end.send: Send to the friend who posted a very specific song story after a breakup.

draft.caption: The sunset was real. The audience was one person.
draft.alt_text: A seven-slide text post arguing that we often post Instagram stories to send one specific person a message without messaging them, and check the viewer list to see if they watched. It describes opening your own sunset story again and again to scan for one name, and gives typical examples: a breakup song story, a gym selfie or new job post meant for an ex or old boss, and a party story meant for the friend who didn't invite you. It notes that such stories go up at the hour that person is usually online, and some get deleted if the wrong person views first. It explains that a story is safer than a text because it is deniable, works like a read receipt you never asked for, and that when the name doesn't appear, people post a second story instead of texting. It notes that in 2018 Instagram said the viewer list is sorted by several signals, so a name's position says nothing about that person. It ends by asking the reader to name who their last five stories were really for, saying the audience was never the viewer count but one name in it.
